summary:
Tunisia is a country in active legal and police hostility toward trans people, and trans visitors should treat it as a destination to avoid. Penal Code Article 230 punishes same-sex conduct with up to three years' imprisonment, and Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression; enforcement falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.

The scale of enforcement is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, and the sweep is national in character rather than confined to any one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released after their sentences were reduced.

Custody itself is a site of specific harm for trans women. The Intersection Association reports that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity that begins at arrest and continues through sentencing. Local documentation describes severe abuse for trans women held in men's facilities.

Legal gender recognition is not available as a reliable route. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, and recognition remains unsettled below the Court of Cassation, decided case by case and frequently denied.
tangentialFactors:
Police conduct in these cases has a documented record. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 March 2016 that at least seven men were prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months, all convicted under Penal Code Article 230; the detainees interviewed described beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police.

Tunisia has made an international commitment that has not changed the law. In 2017 the government pledged to the United Nations to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay statute itself, a point Kapitalis made at the time: a pledge of this kind decriminalises nothing. The gap between procedural commitment and substantive law is the pattern a visitor should expect, since the underlying offences and their penalties remain in force.

The trajectory since President Saied's 2021 concentration of power has been toward harsher application rather than liberalisation, and the 2024–2025 arrests sit within that direction of travel rather than as an isolated episode.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Tunisia is pursued through the courts with no settled rule. The Tunis Court of First Instance's April 2023 refusal to recognise a transgender man came after it weighed contradictory lower-court judgments, including case No. 12304/2018, and found no consistent precedent; the outcome for any individual petition therefore depends on the bench that hears it, and the question remains open below the Court of Cassation.

For transgender women already in the prison system, the identity recorded at arrest governs what follows. The Intersection Association's November 2024 documentation describes continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system, with former names and birth gender carried through detention records, arrest paperwork and court hearings, so a resident facing custody should expect to be named and classified against her gender at every stage.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether forced anal examinations have in fact stopped since the 2017 pledge to the United Nations is unresolved in these sources; the inventory records the commitment and the retention of the statute, not compliance in practice.

The outcome of any appeal of the April 2023 gender-recognition refusal to the Court of Cassation is not sourced here, as is the current state of any consolidated precedent on recognition.

The grounds for the sentence reductions that led to the release of four people on 5 February 2025 are not stated in the inventory.

No source in this inventory addresses visa or border screening, identity-document checks at entry, healthcare access, or facilities rules for trans visitors in Tunisia; these are not sourced rather than established as safe or absent.
